title: Fossils
objectives: Distinguish body fossils from trace fossils and explain preservation.
Use index fossils and superposition to correlate strata.
Evaluate the incompleteness and sampling biases of the fossil record.

glossary.definition: Preserved remains or evidence of an organism from the past.
Preserved evidence of biological activity rather than the body itself.
Fossil useful for correlation because its species had a short geological range and wide distribution.

slides.title: Evidence of past life
slides.html: Fossils include preserved parts of organisms and evidence of their activities. Bones, teeth and shells are body remains; footprints, burrows and coprolites record activity. Palaeontology studies these records to reconstruct past organisms and environments. A fossil is evidence requiring interpretation: a track records movement, for example, but does not necessarily identify the exact species that produced it.

slides.title: Why preservation is uncommon
slides.html: Most organisms decay or are consumed before burial. Rapid burial and resistant hard parts can improve the chance of preservation, while later erosion, heat and deformation may destroy what formed. Discovery adds another filter because accessible rocks and search effort are uneven. The fossil record is therefore a biased sample, not a complete census of every organism that once lived.

diagram.caption: Each stage filters the evidence available. Many organisms leave no discoverable fossil.

slides.title: Different preservation pathways
slides.html: A mould records an impression or cavity left by an organism; a cast forms when that space is filled. Mineral-rich water can deposit minerals in pore spaces, and replacement can substitute minerals for original material. Some remains survive in ice or resin. These pathways preserve different kinds of information, so a fossil’s formation process affects which anatomical claims are justified.

slides.title: Fossils within strata
slides.html: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower layers were deposited before layers above them. Fossils can therefore help establish the relative order of organisms or events. This inference requires geological context: folding, faulting, erosion or transport may complicate the sequence. A loose fossil found on a slope should not automatically be assigned to the nearest exposed layer.

diagram.caption: Hypothetical undisturbed layers illustrate relative ordering only. Symbols do not identify actual fossil species or numerical ages.

slides.title: Index fossils and correlation
slides.html: An effective index fossil represents a species that was widespread but existed for a comparatively short geological interval. Finding it in separate exposures can support correlation of those layers. The rock types need not match, because different environments can accumulate different sediments at the same time. Correlation establishes comparable age intervals, not necessarily exactly simultaneous deposition to a single year.

slides.title: Geological time
slides.html: The geological time scale organises Earth history into nested intervals, including eons, eras, periods and epochs. Boundaries are established using geological evidence and are calibrated numerically. The Cenozoic began about 66 million years ago and includes the Paleogene, Neogene and Quaternary periods. Interval durations are unequal; the hierarchy is not a set of evenly spaced time bins.

slides.title: Interpreting patterns without a progress ladder
slides.html: Fossils document appearances, extinctions and changes in distributions and anatomical features. These patterns support branching evolutionary histories, not an inevitable march towards greater complexity or towards humans. A lineage’s first known fossil sets a minimum known occurrence; earlier members may not have been preserved or discovered. Absence from one deposit can also reflect local environmental conditions rather than global extinction.

slides.title: Multiple lines of evidence
slides.html: A convincing reconstruction combines morphology, rock context, numerical dating where suitable and comparisons among sites. Fossils can inform past habitats through assemblages of organisms and sedimentary features, while preserving uncertainty about exact behaviour. Microbial structures such as stromatolites provide evidence about early ecosystems, but identifying very ancient biological signals requires careful exclusion of non-biological alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which specimen is a trace fossil?
options: A preserved tooth
A mineralised shell
A fossilised footprint
A skull fragment
feedback: A tooth is a body fossil.
A shell is a preserved body structure.
A footprint records an organism’s activity rather than its body.
A skull fragment is a body remain.
questions.explanation: A footprint records an organism’s activity rather than its body.

questions.prompt: Which combination makes an index fossil especially useful?
options: Rare locally and present for nearly all Earth history
Only found at one site and impossible to identify
Always in rocks of identical colour
Widely distributed and restricted to a short geological interval
feedback: A very long range gives poor time resolution.
Restricted distribution and uncertain identification hinder correlation.
Rock colour is not the defining criterion.
Wide distribution permits correlation and a short range narrows the age interval.
questions.explanation: Wide distribution permits correlation and a short range narrows the age interval.

questions.prompt: What does a cast preserve?
options: Material filling a mould left by an organism
Only the unchanged original DNA
Only the organism’s behaviour in life
A complete population census
feedback: A cast is a filled impression or cavity replicating aspects of form.
Fossil casts do not necessarily preserve DNA.
A cast may replicate form without revealing behaviour.
One preservation type is not a census of a population.
questions.explanation: A cast is a filled impression or cavity replicating aspects of form.

questions.prompt: An organism is absent from one fossil deposit. What conclusion is warranted?
options: It never existed anywhere.
Local absence alone does not establish global extinction.
It had no hard parts in every environment.
Its descendants could not evolve.
feedback: One deposit is not the entire fossil record.
Preservation, environment and sampling can all affect local occurrence.
The absence does not identify a universal anatomical condition.
Local fossil absence does not establish absence of descendants.
questions.explanation: Preservation, environment and sampling can all affect local occurrence.

questions.prompt: Explain why the fossil record is incomplete and why the gaps are not randomly distributed.
questions.model: Organisms may decay before burial, lack resistant parts or live where sediment rarely accumulates. Fossils that form can later be destroyed by erosion, heating or deformation, and many surviving deposits are inaccessible or unsearched. These processes favour some organisms and environments over others. The record therefore contains systematic preservation and discovery biases, rather than an equally complete sample of every habitat and lineage.
criteria: Explain failure to preserve.
Explain later destruction or incomplete discovery.
Link biases to differences among organisms or environments.

questions.prompt: Two distant layers contain the same short-lived, widespread fossil species but different rock types. Explain the age inference and one limitation.
questions.model: The shared index fossil supports correlation within the geological interval when that species existed. Different rock types can form at the same time in different depositional environments, so lithological difference does not necessarily contradict correlation. The inference depends on correct fossil identification and geological context; reworked fossils can be transported from older deposits. The layers need not have formed at exactly the same instant.
criteria: Use fossil range to support correlation.
Explain why rock types may differ.
State identification, reworking or precision limits.

summary: Body and trace fossils preserve different evidence.
Formation, survival and discovery all bias the record.
Index fossils support correlation across exposures.
Fossil histories are branching and uncertain, not ladders of progress.
sourceNotes: Updated Cenozoic boundary/periods against International Commission on Stratigraphy: https://stratigraphy.org/chart/
Avoided source claims that fossil history necessarily trends towards complexity or that every stromatolite-like structure is unequivocally biological.

title: Absolute Age and Relative Age
objectives: Distinguish ordering events from estimating numerical ages.
Apply superposition, cross-cutting and fossil correlation with stated assumptions.
Explain why dating methods must match material and geological context.

glossary.definition: An age expressed as older or younger than another event or material.
An age estimate in years with an associated uncertainty.
Time over which half the parent atoms in a radioactive population decay.

slides.title: Two complementary age questions
slides.html: Relative dating places events in order. Numerical dating estimates time in years, often reported with an uncertainty range. Knowing that one fossil is older than another does not itself tell us their age difference. Conversely, a laboratory date is meaningful only after identifying what event the measured material records, such as mineral crystallisation or the death of an organism.

slides.title: Superposition
slides.html: In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower strata were deposited before the strata above them. This principle gives a relative order rather than a numerical date. Deformation can overturn or repeat layers, and erosion can remove parts of the sequence. Geological observations must therefore establish whether the simple model is appropriate before ordering the fossils it contains.

diagram.caption: Hypothetical undisturbed column. The ordering is relative; equal layer thickness does not imply equal deposition time.

slides.title: Cross-cutting and missing time
slides.html: An intrusion or fault that cuts a rock unit formed after the unit it cuts. An erosional surface may represent missing time between deposits, so successive preserved layers need not form continuously. Combining cross-cutting relationships, superposition and fossil correlation creates a stronger event sequence than relying on vertical position alone. A nearby rock body is not necessarily the same age as a fossil.

slides.title: Correlating separate deposits
slides.html: A widespread species with a short geological range can serve as an index fossil. Comparable occurrences help correlate layers at different sites, provided that the fossils were not reworked from older deposits. A correlation narrows a time interval but is not an exact date for each individual organism. Several independent markers can improve the reliability of a proposed match.

slides.title: Fluorine uptake as relative evidence
slides.html: Buried bone can take up fluoride from surrounding water. Under comparable local conditions, differences in fluorine content may help assess relative time in the ground. Uptake also depends on groundwater chemistry, permeability, temperature and the bone itself. Bones from different environments cannot simply be ranked using fluorine concentration alone, and the measurement is not a universal clock giving years.

slides.title: Radioactive clocks
slides.html: A radioactive parent isotope transforms into daughter products at a characteristic statistical rate. After each half-life, half of the previously remaining parent population remains. The sequence is exponential: one half, one quarter, one eighth and so on. Suitable isotope measurements can therefore produce numerical age estimates, provided the initial conditions and later history of the sample are adequately understood.

diagram.caption: Ideal closed-system model: parent fractions after successive half-lives are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16. This is not a constant number of atoms lost each interval.

slides.title: Choose material and method together
slides.html: Carbon-14 dating is used for suitable once-living material over recent geological time, commonly up to around 50,000 years. Much older fossils may be bracketed by dated volcanic layers rather than dated directly. Long-lived isotope systems can date appropriate minerals. Contamination, loss or gain of material, and the event that reset the clock must all be considered.

slides.title: Combining dates into a bracket
slides.html: Suppose a hypothetical fossil-bearing layer lies above volcanic ash dated 1.8 million years and below ash dated 1.5 million years. If the layers are undisturbed and the fossil is not reworked, the fossil lies between those ages. The measurements date the ash events; the fossil’s inferred interval also depends on its stratigraphic association and the uncertainty of each date.

questions.prompt: Which statement gives a relative age?
options: The layer formed 1.50 ± 0.02 million years ago.
The fossil is older than the overlying ash layer.
The sample contains 25% of its initial parent isotope.
The laboratory measured a mass of 5.0 grams.
feedback: This is a numerical age with uncertainty.
This orders two events without assigning years.
An isotope proportion needs a model and half-life to become an age.
Mass does not give an age relationship.
questions.explanation: This orders two events without assigning years.

questions.prompt: A fault cuts two sedimentary layers. What is the simplest supported relative relationship?
options: The fault is older than both layers.
The layers and fault must all have formed simultaneously.
The faulting event is younger than the layers it cuts.
The fault determines the exact numerical age of each layer.
feedback: The cutting event must follow formation of the material it cuts.
A cross-cutting relationship indicates a sequence.
This is the cross-cutting principle, subject to correct geological interpretation.
Ordering is not a numerical measurement.
questions.explanation: This is the cross-cutting principle, subject to correct geological interpretation.

questions.prompt: In an ideal decay model, what fraction of the original parent isotope remains after three half-lives?
questions.hint: Multiply one half by itself three times.
questions.explanation: Remaining fraction = (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 0.125.

questions.prompt: Why can fluorine content not be used as one universal numerical bone clock?
options: Fluoride uptake depends on local conditions and the properties of the bone.
Fluorine is a parent isotope with the same half-life in every bone.
All bones acquire exactly the same fluoride concentration immediately.
Groundwater has no influence on the process.
feedback: Chemical environment and material differences affect uptake, limiting direct comparisons.
This is a chemical-uptake comparison, not a universal radioactive clock.
Uptake is not an immediate identical change in every specimen.
Groundwater chemistry is central to fluoride uptake.
questions.explanation: Chemical environment and material differences affect uptake, limiting direct comparisons.

questions.prompt: Explain why an ash layer date is not automatically the exact age of a fossil found nearby.
questions.model: The measurement may date mineral formation or another clock-setting event in the ash, not the organism’s death. The ash and fossil need a demonstrated stratigraphic relationship. The fossil may lie above or below the dated layer or may have been reworked. Numerical uncertainty and disturbance must also be considered. Appropriate layers can bracket a fossil age, but physical proximity alone does not establish identical ages.
criteria: Identify the event actually dated.
Require geological association rather than proximity.
Explain bracketing, reworking or uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A fossil lies between lower ash dated 1.8 Ma and upper ash dated 1.5 Ma. State the inferred interval and two assumptions.
questions.model: The fossil-bearing deposit is inferred to be younger than 1.8 Ma and older than 1.5 Ma. This assumes an undisturbed sequence in which the ash layers and fossil occupy their original relative positions, and that the fossil has not been reworked from an older deposit. The ash dates must be suitable estimates of their depositional context, and their reported uncertainties should be retained.
criteria: Give the correct younger/older bounds.
State undisturbed stratigraphy.
Identify reworking or date-event/uncertainty limitations.

summary: Relative dates order events; numerical dates estimate years.
Simple stratigraphic rules require geological context.
Chemical uptake and radiometric clocks have different assumptions.
Fossil ages can be constrained indirectly by dated layers.
sourceNotes: Did not reproduce the source’s confusion between ancient zircon mineral grains and the age of the surrounding rock body.

title: Radiometric Dating
objectives: Calculate ideal ages from parent fractions and half-lives.
Compare carbon-14 and potassium–argon dating for appropriate materials.
Evaluate calibration, contamination and clock-resetting assumptions.

glossary.definition: Radioactive isotope whose decay is used in an age model.
Product formed through radioactive decay.
A sample that has retained the relevant parent and daughter material after the event being dated.

slides.title: The decay principle
slides.html: Radiometric dating combines isotope measurements with a known decay rate. Individual atoms decay unpredictably, but large populations follow a stable statistical pattern. A half-life halves the number of parent atoms remaining, rather than removing a fixed number each interval. The measured isotope system must correspond to an identifiable event and remain sufficiently closed afterwards for the chosen model to apply.

slides.title: Working with half-lives
slides.html: In an ideal model, 50% parent remaining corresponds to one half-life, 25% to two and 12.5% to three. Multiply the number of elapsed half-lives by the stated half-life to calculate time. These simple classroom problems assume the original parent proportion is known and no relevant material has entered or left. Real measurements also require uncertainty analysis.

diagram.caption: Ideal parent-isotope fractions. The fraction halves repeatedly, producing exponential decay rather than a straight-line decrease.

slides.title: Carbon-14 enters living systems
slides.html: Carbon-14 is produced in the atmosphere through interactions involving cosmic-ray-generated neutrons and nitrogen. It becomes part of atmospheric carbon dioxide and enters food webs through carbon uptake. While alive, organisms exchange carbon with their environment. After death, this exchange largely stops and remaining carbon-14 decays, allowing suitable preserved material to be dated.

slides.title: What a radiocarbon age refers to
slides.html: Radiocarbon estimates the time since carbon exchange ceased for the sampled material, not necessarily when people used an artefact made from it. Old wood can be reused long after the tree grew. Contamination by younger or older carbon can also bias a measurement. Sample selection and archaeological context are therefore as important as the laboratory’s ability to detect carbon-14.

slides.title: Range and calibration
slides.html: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years. After many half-lives the remaining amount becomes difficult to distinguish from background and contamination, so routine useful ages are commonly limited to around 50,000 years. Atmospheric carbon-14 levels have varied, requiring calibration. Dinosaur fossils are far too old for radiocarbon dating; a measured modern-carbon trace would not date the dinosaur.

slides.title: Potassium–argon dating
slides.html: Potassium-40 has a half-life of about 1.25 billion years and decays through more than one branch, including a branch producing argon-40. Potassium–argon dating measures appropriate potassium-bearing minerals and accumulated radiogenic argon. Cooling can allow a mineral system to retain argon, providing a clock-setting event. Argon loss or inherited excess argon can complicate the inferred age.

diagram.caption: Simplified potassium–argon clock. This dates an appropriate mineral event, not automatically the death of an associated fossil.

slides.title: Other mineral clocks
slides.html: Fission-track dating uses damage trails produced by spontaneous uranium fission in suitable minerals or glass. Track accumulation, uranium content and thermal history matter because heating can erase tracks. Other isotope systems, such as uranium–lead and rubidium–strontium, address different materials and histories. No single method is suitable for every age, substance or geological event.

slides.title: Combining methods and evidence
slides.html: A fossil can be constrained using dated volcanic horizons, relative stratigraphy and independent checks. Agreement among appropriate methods strengthens an interpretation, while disagreement can reveal disturbance, contamination or different events recorded by different minerals. Reporting an age with uncertainty and assumptions is more informative than presenting a numerical result as exact. Better sensitivity does not remove the need for a valid model.

questions.prompt: An ideal sample has 25% of its original carbon-14 remaining. Using a half-life of 5730 years, calculate its uncalibrated model age.
questions.hint: 25% is one quarter, corresponding to two halvings.
questions.explanation: Two half-lives have elapsed: 2 × 5730 = 11,460 years. This is an ideal, uncalibrated model result.

questions.prompt: Which sample is the best candidate for carbon-14 dating?
options: A mineral crystallised two billion years ago.
A dinosaur skeleton tens of millions of years old.
Preserved charcoal from a hearth several thousand years old.
A volcanic crystal known to contain no organic carbon.
feedback: Carbon-14 is unsuitable for such ancient mineral formation.
The age is far beyond the useful radiocarbon range.
Suitable charcoal retains once-living carbon within a useful radiocarbon age range.
A mineral without appropriate carbon is not a suitable radiocarbon target.
questions.explanation: Suitable charcoal retains once-living carbon within a useful radiocarbon age range.

questions.prompt: Why is potassium–argon useful in some fossil contexts?
options: It directly measures an organism’s time of death in all bones.
All potassium-40 becomes argon-40 immediately.
Argon can never escape from any material.
Suitable volcanic minerals can date horizons associated with fossil-bearing layers.
feedback: Its usual target is suitable mineral material, not all fossil bone.
Potassium-40 decays over time through more than one branch.
Argon retention is an assumption requiring geological evaluation.
Mineral ages and stratigraphic association can constrain fossil ages indirectly.
questions.explanation: Mineral ages and stratigraphic association can constrain fossil ages indirectly.

questions.prompt: An ancient wooden beam was reused centuries later. What does its carbon-14 age principally relate to?
options: The dated carbon’s cessation of exchange, not necessarily the reuse event.
The exact date of the building’s latest renovation.
The age of every object found beside the beam.
The date at which the wood was first measured.
feedback: The age of the wood’s carbon can predate its later human use.
Reuse does not reset the carbon clock.
Association does not make all objects the same age.
Laboratory measurement date is not the sample’s radiocarbon age.
questions.explanation: The age of the wood’s carbon can predate its later human use.

questions.prompt: Explain why measuring a very small amount of carbon-14 does not automatically provide a valid age for a dinosaur fossil.
questions.model: Dinosaur fossils are vastly older than the ordinary useful radiocarbon range, so their original carbon-14 would have decayed to amounts far below practical interpretation. Small detected amounts can arise from background or contamination. A suitable dating method must match material, age range and geological history. Dating associated mineral horizons with appropriate long-lived isotope systems can constrain an ancient fossil without pretending that radiocarbon measures its age.
criteria: State the age-range mismatch.
Identify contamination or background.
Suggest suitable indirect mineral dating with context.

questions.prompt: Describe the assumptions behind a simple half-life calculation and why a real date needs more information.
questions.model: A classroom calculation assumes a known initial parent amount, a specified half-life and retention of relevant material after a clock-setting event. A real analysis must determine what event the sample records, check contamination or parent/daughter loss, and estimate measurement uncertainty. Some methods also need calibration or correction for initial daughter material. Numerical precision alone cannot compensate for invalid sample history or an unsuitable isotope system.
criteria: Identify initial amount and repeated halving.
Identify closure and the event being dated.
Explain calibration, correction or uncertainty.

summary: Parent fractions halve repeatedly rather than decreasing linearly.
Carbon-14 targets suitable recent once-living material.
Potassium–argon commonly dates appropriate volcanic mineral events.
Calibration, closure and context determine validity.
sourceNotes: Corrected source errors: Jack Hills zircons are billions, not millions, of years old; mineral ages are not automatically the enclosing rock’s depositional age. Did not retain outdated universal lower cut-offs for K–Ar.

title: Changes in Technology
objectives: Explain how instruments extend the evidence available for evolutionary study.
Distinguish measurements from the inferences made using them.
Evaluate contamination, uncertainty and computational assumptions.

glossary.definition: Ability to distinguish nearby details as separate.
Instrument that separates and measures ions according to mass-to-charge ratio.
Computational analysis and management of biological data.

slides.title: Technology changes the evidence available
slides.html: Scientific explanations are constrained by what can be observed and measured. Improved instruments can reveal previously inaccessible features, measure smaller samples or compare larger data sets. New results may refine a date or alter a proposed relationship. Technology does not make interpretation automatic: researchers still need appropriate sampling, controls and models that connect measurements with biological or geological claims.

slides.title: Relative sequences and numerical clocks
slides.html: Stratigraphy establishes relationships among deposits, while isotope measurements can calibrate suitable events numerically. Mass spectrometers measure isotope ratios using ions, allowing age models to be applied to carefully selected material. A more precise ratio is useful only when the relevant clock-setting event and later sample history are understood. An instrument does not itself decide whether a fossil has been reworked.

diagram.caption: Isotope measurements are interpreted using a decay model. Improved measurement precision does not remove the need to check sample history and assumptions.

slides.title: Magnification is not resolution
slides.html: Magnification enlarges an image; resolution determines whether nearby features can be distinguished. Enlarging an already blurred image does not recover missing detail. Electron microscopy can reveal fine surface or internal features beyond ordinary light-microscope resolution, depending on preparation and method. Specimen treatment can also create artefacts, so an image must be interpreted in the context of how it was obtained.

slides.title: Microscopy and fossil interpretation
slides.html: Fine features on teeth and bones can inform hypotheses about wear, diet or processing. A groove that resembles a tool mark is not automatically proof of butchery: trampling, abrasion and other processes may leave marks. Researchers compare form, position and associated evidence. Better imaging can test alternatives, but behaviour remains an inference from preserved traces rather than a directly observed past event.

slides.title: DNA amplification and sequencing
slides.html: PCR can increase the quantity of a targeted DNA region, while sequencing identifies the order of bases. These methods permit comparisons among suitable samples, including some ancient remains. Very old DNA is often fragmented and vulnerable to contamination. Controls, independent replication and characteristic damage patterns help evaluate authenticity; amplification alone cannot distinguish ancient DNA from a modern contaminant.

diagram.caption: Simplified molecular-evidence workflow. Actual procedures differ with material and method; not all fossils retain usable DNA.

slides.title: Comparative biochemical evidence
slides.html: Protein sequences and other biochemical characters can be compared where suitable evidence is preserved. Similarity in corresponding molecules can support common ancestry, but not every sequence position changes at the same rate. A reliable analysis considers which molecules and positions are comparable, functional constraints and alternative explanations. An apparent difference may also arise from measurement or reconstruction error rather than genuine evolutionary change.

slides.title: Bioinformatics and databases
slides.html: Genome comparisons involve data too extensive for unaided manual analysis. Software can align corresponding sequences, search databases and evaluate relationship models. The resulting tree depends on data quality, alignment, sampling and model assumptions. A computer-generated result should therefore be interpreted as an evidence-based hypothesis with uncertainty, not as an unquestionable answer produced merely because software was used.

slides.title: Updating an explanation responsibly
slides.html: When new measurements conflict with an older model, first evaluate sample identity, methods and uncertainty. Consistent independent evidence may justify revising the model. Revision is a normal part of scientific work, not evidence that all earlier conclusions were arbitrary. A strong account names the technology, explains the new kind of evidence it provides and states the limit of the inference it supports.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes resolution from magnification?
options: Magnification always reveals every small feature.
Resolution concerns separating close details; magnification concerns image size.
Resolution is the size of the screen only.
The terms describe exactly the same measurement.
feedback: An enlarged blur does not gain resolved detail.
These describe distinct aspects of imaging.
Screen size alone does not define resolving power.
The two terms are not interchangeable.
questions.explanation: These describe distinct aspects of imaging.

questions.prompt: Why are contamination controls important when analysing ancient DNA?
options: All amplified DNA must be ancient.
PCR gives an exact fossil date.
Modern DNA can be amplified and mistaken for evidence from the specimen.
Controls alter the ancestry of the sample.
feedback: Amplification does not establish the age or origin of the DNA.
PCR amplifies target DNA rather than directly dating a fossil.
Contaminants may produce strong signals, requiring authentication and controls.
Controls test procedures; they do not change historical ancestry.
questions.explanation: Contaminants may produce strong signals, requiring authentication and controls.

questions.prompt: What does a mass spectrometer contribute to suitable radiometric dating?
options: It directly reads the fossil species name.
It decides whether layers are overturned.
It measures bone length only.
It measures isotope information used in a justified age model.
feedback: Species identification requires other evidence.
Geological structure needs contextual observations.
That is not its isotope-analysis role.
Measured isotope ratios can inform a clock model after assumptions are evaluated.
questions.explanation: Measured isotope ratios can inform a clock model after assumptions are evaluated.

questions.prompt: A program returns a phylogenetic tree. What is the best next interpretation?
options: Evaluate sampling, sequence alignment and model assumptions.
Accept the tree because computers cannot make mistakes.
Assume every branch has an exact known date.
Conclude that no other data can revise it.
feedback: Computational outputs depend on the evidence and assumptions supplied.
Software and input data can contain errors or limitations.
Branch dates require additional calibration and modelling.
Further evidence can support or revise a relationship hypothesis.
questions.explanation: Computational outputs depend on the evidence and assumptions supplied.

questions.prompt: Explain how electron microscopy can improve an evolutionary interpretation without making the interpretation certain.
questions.model: Higher resolving power can reveal fine features such as surface marks or tooth-wear patterns that are difficult to distinguish with ordinary light microscopy. These observations may help test hypotheses about function or behaviour. However, preparation artefacts and alternative processes can produce similar appearances. The inference therefore requires comparisons, context and independent evidence rather than treating a detailed image as direct observation of a past behaviour.
criteria: Distinguish increased detail from enlargement alone.
Link detail to a specific evolutionary question.
Explain an alternative process or methodological limitation.

questions.prompt: Explain why technological improvement can lead to revision of a fossil’s age or relationship.
questions.model: An improved method may measure isotope ratios more precisely, reveal overlooked anatomy or recover authenticated molecular evidence. These results can narrow age estimates or challenge a proposed relationship. Researchers must first check sample association, contamination and analytical assumptions. Agreement among independent evidence can justify updating the model. The revision is a response to better evidence, not an automatic consequence of replacing an older instrument with a newer one.
criteria: Name a technology and the evidence it supplies.
Connect new evidence with a revised inference.
Include a validity or uncertainty check.

summary: New instruments extend observation and measurement.
Resolution differs from magnification.
Molecular evidence requires authenticity controls.
Computational analyses remain conditional on data and models.
sourceNotes: Corrected source reversal of carbon isotope ratio: after death carbon-14 relative to stable carbon decreases, not the reverse.
Avoided the source’s incorrect phrase amino acid sequences in DNA: DNA has base sequences and proteins have amino acid sequences.

title: Activity — Fossils Give a Timeline for Life on Earth
objectives: Construct and interpret a scaled timeline with consistent units.
Distinguish first known fossil occurrence from evolutionary origin.
Explain how fossil and environmental evidence constrain accounts of Earth history.

glossary.definition: Millions of years before the present.
Billions of years before the present.
Earliest occurrence currently demonstrated by available evidence, not necessarily the true origin.

slides.title: A timeline is a scaled model
slides.html: A geological timeline places events along a time axis using a stated scale. Equal distances represent equal durations, even when the events chosen are very different. A useful timeline labels its units and reference direction clearly. Writing events in order is not sufficient if spacing is intended to communicate how much time separates them.

slides.title: Converting units before plotting
slides.html: Convert all ages to one unit before calculating positions. One billion years equals one thousand million years, so 3.5 Ga becomes 3500 Ma. Mixing the numbers 3.5 and 3500 without their units would misplace the event by a factor of a thousand. Keep approximate estimates and uncertainty labels when the source evidence does not support an exact time.

slides.title: A worked scale example
slides.html: In a hypothetical exercise, a 100 Ma interval is drawn as a 20 cm line. Each centimetre represents 5 Ma. An event at 25 Ma belongs 5 cm from the present end, while an event at 80 Ma belongs 16 cm from that end. These positions follow proportional calculation; they are not chosen to give equally spaced event labels.

diagram.caption: Invented teaching ages for a scale calculation. The present is 0 Ma; this is not a record of named biological events.

slides.title: Why recent events cluster
slides.html: Earth history spans billions of years, while the history of our own species occupies a much shorter interval. On one linear axis, recent events can be crowded near the present. A clearly labelled enlarged inset can show those events in detail. Changing scale without stating it would distort the apparent duration; an inset must not be mistaken for a continuation at the original scale.

slides.title: Fossils and minimum known ages
slides.html: The oldest known fossil assigned to a group shows that the group existed by that time, assuming identification and dating are sound. It does not prove that the group originated at that precise moment. Earlier populations may have left no discovered record. New fossils can therefore extend a group’s known range without implying that scientists previously observed its true moment of origin.

slides.title: Explaining gaps in the record
slides.html: A sparse fossil interval can reflect preservation conditions, limited exposed rock or incomplete search effort. Early microbial life also leaves evidence that can be difficult to distinguish from non-biological structures. It is misleading to claim that fossils record only a fixed final percentage of Earth history. Evidence extends deep into the past, although its abundance, form and certainty vary greatly.

diagram.caption: Conceptual contrast in evidence quality, not a dated measured sequence. Sparse evidence does not demonstrate that no organisms existed.

slides.title: Environmental reconstruction
slides.html: Fossil pollen, plant remains, animal assemblages and sediments can jointly indicate past environments. For example, a change in pollen assemblages may support a change in vegetation, while sedimentary evidence helps test climate or water conditions. One fossil alone rarely determines a complete climate. Transport, local habitat differences and preservation bias must be considered when connecting organisms to environmental history.

slides.title: Evidence-based timeline conclusions
slides.html: An interpretation should distinguish an observation, its date estimate and its biological meaning. A fossil occurrence can document a group at a place and time; claiming a migration, global extinction or evolutionary origin requires additional evidence. Good timelines retain missing intervals, uncertainty and source distinctions. They organise evidence for a historical explanation rather than turning every first appearance into a certain origin date.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical 100 Ma interval occupies 20 cm. How many centimetres from the present end should a 25 Ma event be plotted?
questions.hint: Find centimetres per million years, then multiply by 25.

questions.prompt: Convert 3.5 billion years into millions of years.
questions.hint: One billion equals one thousand million.
questions.explanation: 3.5 × 1000 = 3500 million years.

questions.prompt: What does a securely dated oldest known fossil of a group establish?
options: The group certainly originated on that exact day.
The group had no ancestors.
The group existed by that date, but may have originated earlier.
All fossils of the group have that same age.
feedback: First discovery does not identify an exact origin moment.
A dated occurrence does not remove an evolutionary ancestry.
It supplies a minimum known age for the group’s existence.
A group may occur across a range of ages.
questions.explanation: It supplies a minimum known age for the group’s existence.

questions.prompt: Why might a detailed inset be needed for recent events on an Earth-history timeline?
options: All geological intervals have equal durations.
Recent events must be older than ancient events.
Insets eliminate all dating uncertainty.
A long linear scale can crowd short recent intervals near the present.
feedback: Geological intervals are not all equal.
The present-end ordering remains unchanged.
Changing display scale does not remove uncertainty.
An explicitly labelled inset enlarges a crowded part without silently changing the main scale.
questions.explanation: An explicitly labelled inset enlarges a crowded part without silently changing the main scale.

questions.prompt: Explain why the first known fossil appearance of a group should not be labelled unconditionally as its evolutionary origin.
questions.model: The oldest demonstrated occurrence shows that the group existed at least by that time. Fossil formation, survival and discovery are incomplete, so earlier populations might not be represented in available collections. Identification and dating also have uncertainty. A new find can extend the known range. A timeline should therefore label the first known occurrence separately from a hypothesised origin rather than treating the two as identical.
criteria: State what the fossil establishes.
Explain preservation or discovery incompleteness.
Distinguish known occurrence from inferred origin.

questions.prompt: Describe how a scaled fossil timeline should communicate both time and uncertainty.
questions.model: Use one stated unit and a labelled time direction, calculate event positions proportionally and preserve gaps between dates. Clearly identify approximate ages or ranges rather than adding unsupported precision. If recent events need an enlarged inset, give its separate scale. Distinguish fossils, geological events and inferred origins in the labels, because the age of a sampled material is not automatically the exact time of every associated biological event.
criteria: Describe consistent scale and units.
Retain uncertainty or age ranges.
Identify insets and the event represented by each age.

summary: Scaled distance represents duration, not just event order.
Convert Ga and Ma before plotting.
First known fossils do not establish exact origin times.
Environmental interpretations combine several evidence types.
sourceNotes: Did not reuse the source’s outdated dates or misleading claim that fossils show only 15% of Earth history. Numerical timeline data in this lesson are explicitly hypothetical.

title: Historical Development of Evolution Theories
objectives: Compare historical explanations for evolutionary change.
Explain natural selection using inherited variation and differential reproduction.
Distinguish divergent and convergent outcomes without attributing intention.

glossary.definition: Differences in reproductive success associated with heritable variation in a particular environment.
Relative contribution of offspring to subsequent generations in a given environment.
Diversification of an ancestral lineage into forms occupying different ecological roles.

slides.title: Historical explanations changed
slides.html: Naturalists compared living organisms, fossils and geographical distributions before the molecular basis of inheritance was understood. Observations of extinct forms and differences among populations challenged the idea that all species remained unchanged. Several explanations were proposed, but historical importance is not the same as modern acceptance. A scientific account evaluates the mechanism and evidence rather than accepting a proposal solely because of its age or author.

slides.title: Lamarck and acquired characteristics
slides.html: Lamarck proposed that use or disuse could modify an individual’s structures and that acquired changes could then be inherited. This differs from selection acting on heritable variation already present in a population. In ordinary evolutionary explanations, an individual’s need or exercise does not directly produce the specific inherited adaptation required by its descendants. Environmental influence on organisms must not be confused with purposeful evolution.

slides.title: Geology and population pressures
slides.html: Geological observations supported a long and changing Earth history, providing time for large cumulative biological changes. Ideas about population growth and limited resources also helped frame competition and unequal survival. These ideas did not themselves specify genes or alleles. Their contribution was to questions and explanatory frameworks that could connect variation, population constraints and historical change.

slides.title: Darwin and Wallace
slides.html: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed explanations of evolution through natural selection. Their ideas were jointly announced in 1858; Darwin’s On the Origin of Species followed in 1859. Both drew on observations of organisms and distributions, not on a modern molecular account of DNA. Later genetics supplied mechanisms of inheritance and variation that could be integrated with selection.

diagram.caption: Historical calendar years. The events mark public presentation and publication, not the first observations underlying evolutionary thought.

slides.title: The mechanism of selection
slides.html: Individuals in a population differ, and some differences are heritable. Under particular conditions, these differences can affect survival and reproductive success. Individuals that contribute more descendants can make associated variants more common in later generations. Selection therefore changes populations across generations; it does not require individuals to foresee a future environment or transform themselves because they need to survive.

diagram.caption: Invented model illustrating an increased frequency of an inherited variant after differential reproduction. It is not a measured historical population or an inevitable numerical outcome.

slides.title: What fitness means
slides.html: Evolutionary fitness concerns reproductive contribution relative to alternatives in a particular environment. Being larger, stronger or longer-lived does not automatically mean greater fitness. A trait’s effect can change with conditions, and advantages can involve trade-offs. The relevant evidence is how a heritable difference influences descendants, not whether the individual seems more impressive or more successful by a human social standard.

slides.title: Divergence and convergence
slides.html: After lineages split, different selection pressures can produce different modifications of inherited features: divergence. Independent lineages experiencing similar functional demands can evolve similar adaptations: convergence. A streamlined shark and dolphin illustrate a functional resemblance without making the dolphin a close shark relative. A shared underlying limb plan can instead support common ancestry despite differences in present function.

slides.title: Historical ideas and modern evidence
slides.html: Modern evolutionary explanations combine population genetics, fossil histories, anatomy, biogeography and molecular evidence. Natural selection is one important process; mutation, genetic drift and gene flow also affect evolution. Historical uncertainty about inheritance is not a current absence of an explanatory mechanism. Likewise, a biological account of reproductive success is not a moral ranking of individuals or human populations.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes natural selection?
options: Individuals deliberately change the genes their offspring need.
Heritable differences influence reproductive success, changing variant frequencies over generations.
Every mutation increases survival.
All individuals acquire identical adaptations during life.
feedback: Selection does not require directed change based on need.
This links inherited variation to differential reproductive contribution.
Mutations can be harmful, neutral or beneficial depending on context.
Selection acts on differences rather than making every individual identical.
questions.explanation: This links inherited variation to differential reproductive contribution.

questions.prompt: What is evolutionary fitness most directly concerned with?
options: Physical strength alone
Longest individual lifespan in every situation
Relative contribution to later generations
Position in a human social hierarchy
feedback: Strength matters only insofar as it influences reproductive contribution.
Longevity alone need not produce more descendants.
Fitness is contextual reproductive success.
A biological measure is not a moral or social ranking.
questions.explanation: Fitness is contextual reproductive success.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly gives the public announcement and Darwin book dates?
feedback: These are a century too early for those events.
The announcement preceded the book.
These do not match the Darwin–Wallace announcement and Origin publication.
Their ideas were jointly announced in 1858 and Origin was published in 1859.
questions.explanation: Their ideas were jointly announced in 1858 and Origin was published in 1859.

questions.prompt: Which explanation illustrates convergence?
options: Separate lineages independently develop similar swimming shapes.
Two descendants retain corresponding ancestral forelimb bones.
An individual passes on stronger muscles simply because it exercised.
A population always evolves towards greater complexity.
feedback: Independent functional similarity is convergence.
This describes shared inherited structure, which can accompany divergence.
This is an acquired-character inheritance claim, not convergence.
Evolution has no universal required direction towards complexity.
questions.explanation: Independent functional similarity is convergence.

questions.prompt: Compare an acquired-character explanation with a natural-selection explanation for a population becoming better suited to a food source.
questions.model: An acquired-character account attributes inherited change to individuals modifying themselves through use or need and passing those modifications on. A selection account begins with heritable variation in the population. Individuals whose variants help them obtain food and reproduce contribute more descendants, so associated variants can become more common over generations. The latter does not require an individual to intentionally produce the change its descendants need.
criteria: State the acquired-character mechanism.
Begin selection with inherited variation.
Link differential reproduction to population change without intention.

questions.prompt: Explain why stronger individuals are not necessarily the fittest in evolutionary terms.
questions.model: Fitness concerns relative reproductive contribution under particular environmental conditions. Greater strength may help in some circumstances, but it can also carry costs and does not guarantee mating, survival of offspring or more descendants. A smaller individual could contribute more surviving offspring than a stronger one. The relevant comparison is the heritable traits’ effects on reproductive success, not a human judgement that strength is inherently superior.
criteria: Define contextual reproductive contribution.
Distinguish strength from reproductive outcome.
Explain a trade-off or contrasting outcome.

summary: Darwin and Wallace independently developed selection explanations.
Selection links inherited differences to reproductive success.
Fitness is not equivalent to strength or social value.
Divergence and convergence describe different evolutionary patterns.
sourceNotes: Avoided the source’s reversed east/west description of Asian and Australian fauna around the Wallace Line and unsupported political analogies.

title: Punctuated Equilibrium
objectives: Distinguish stasis from continuous directional morphological change.
Explain geologically rapid change without implying one-generation transformation.
Evaluate fossil sampling when comparing evolutionary tempo models.

glossary.definition: Little net directional change in the measured morphology over an extended interval.
A pattern of accumulated change along a lineage over time.
A model emphasising long morphological stasis interrupted by relatively rapid change associated with speciation.

slides.title: Patterns of evolutionary tempo
slides.html: Evolutionary tempo concerns the rate and timing of change. Some fossil sequences show accumulated morphological shifts, while others show long intervals of relatively stable form followed by the appearance of different forms. These observations concern patterns through time. They do not by themselves replace the population processes that generate and alter inherited variation, such as mutation, selection and genetic drift.

slides.title: Gradual change within a lineage
slides.html: In a gradual-change model, measured morphology shifts through successive generations and may produce a long series of intermediate forms. This does not mean every character changes at the same rate or every generation shows a visible fossil difference. Adequately sampled sequences are needed to distinguish a sustained directional trend from variation around a stable average.

layers.label: Younger interval
fossils: Form A with larger measured trait

layers.label: Older interval
fossils: Form A with smaller measured trait

diagram.caption: Schematic gradual-trend sequence. Descriptions represent a measured morphological character, not a complete species ancestry claim or real fossil data.

slides.title: Punctuated equilibrium
slides.html: Eldredge and Gould’s punctuated-equilibrium model emphasises morphological stasis through much of a species’ history, with comparatively rapid changes associated with speciation. A new species can appear abruptly in a local fossil sequence even though its origin involved many generations elsewhere. The contrast is with a uniformly slow transformation being recorded throughout the history of every lineage.

slides.title: What stasis does and does not mean
slides.html: Stasis describes the measured pattern of morphology, not the absence of all genetic change or all variation among individuals. A population can retain a broadly similar external form while allele frequencies or unmeasured characters change. Evidence for stasis requires repeated samples across time; a gap containing no fossils cannot demonstrate that the organisms stayed morphologically unchanged throughout that gap.

slides.title: Rapid on a geological scale
slides.html: A change taking many generations can occupy a short interval compared with millions of years of stasis. Geologically rapid therefore does not mean that a fully formed new species appeared instantly or in one birth. The relevant timescale and the sampling resolution must be stated. A coarse rock sequence can compress a lengthy biological process into a seemingly abrupt boundary.

slides.title: A local record can miss the transition
slides.html: Speciation in a small or geographically separated population may occur outside a sampled site. Later arrival of its descendants can produce an abrupt local fossil appearance. Alternatively, erosion or sparse preservation can remove intermediates. These possibilities mean that abrupt appearance requires interpretation; it does not automatically distinguish a real rapid evolutionary episode from an incomplete local record.

diagram.caption: Two kinds of explanation to test. Similar-looking gaps in a local record need not have the same cause.

slides.title: Comparing models with evidence
slides.html: Researchers measure characters, date successive samples and examine geographical distribution. Evidence that apparent stasis persists across well-sampled intervals is stronger than a comparison of only two distant specimens. Independent age constraints help judge whether an apparent transition is short or merely poorly resolved. Different lineages or traits can exhibit different tempo patterns; one example does not establish a universal rule for all organisms.

slides.title: Avoiding a false either-or choice
slides.html: Punctuated patterns and gradual changes are not mutually exclusive descriptions of all evolution. The useful question is which pattern is supported in a particular lineage, character and time interval. Neither pattern requires abandoning natural selection or assuming directed mutation. A careful answer separates observed morphology, inferred tempo, speciation history and the limitations imposed by the fossil record.

questions.prompt: What does morphological stasis mean?
options: No mutations occur anywhere in the population.
The population has no variation among individuals.
There is little net directional change in the measured morphology over an interval.
No organisms reproduce during the interval.
feedback: Genetic changes can occur without a large shift in measured form.
Individuals can vary around a relatively stable morphology.
Stasis describes a morphological pattern through time.
Stasis does not mean absence of reproduction.
questions.explanation: Stasis describes a morphological pattern through time.

questions.prompt: What does geologically rapid change imply?
options: An entire new species must appear in a single birth.
The change must be caused by a purposeful mutation.
The event has no measurable duration.
The interval is short relative to geological comparison times and may contain many generations.
feedback: Geological rapidity is not a one-generation requirement.
Tempo does not require mutation directed by need.
A short interval can still have duration and uncertainty.
The timescale can be brief geologically but long biologically.
questions.explanation: The timescale can be brief geologically but long biologically.

questions.prompt: A gap separates two fossil forms at one site. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Missing samples, migration and evolutionary change must be evaluated before a tempo claim is made.
The gap alone proves every lineage evolves by punctuated equilibrium.
The organisms had no ancestors.
All genetic evolution stopped during the gap.
feedback: A local gap has multiple possible explanations requiring further evidence.
One incomplete local record cannot establish a universal pattern.
An abrupt sampled appearance does not remove ancestry.
The absence of samples does not demonstrate genetic stasis.
questions.explanation: A local gap has multiple possible explanations requiring further evidence.

questions.prompt: Which observation best supports stasis rather than merely missing evidence?
options: Only one fossil has ever been found.
Many dated samples show similar measured morphology across a long interval.
A rock interval contains no fossils at all.
Two specimens are labelled without their ages.
feedback: One specimen cannot establish a time pattern.
Repeated dated samples can document persistence of a morphological pattern.
An empty interval cannot show what the organisms looked like.
Without temporal placement, the comparison cannot establish stasis.
questions.explanation: Repeated dated samples can document persistence of a morphological pattern.

questions.prompt: Explain why punctuated equilibrium does not require a new species to arise in one generation.
questions.model: Punctuated equilibrium concerns change that is relatively rapid on a geological timescale compared with longer intervals of morphological stasis. Such a transition can still involve many generations and population processes. Speciation may occur in a separate population and be poorly represented at the sampled site. An abrupt local fossil appearance is therefore not evidence that all changes occurred instantly in one individual.
criteria: Distinguish geological and generational timescales.
Link the pattern to population change or speciation.
Explain local sampling or geography.

questions.prompt: Explain how incomplete preservation can resemble rapid evolutionary change, and identify evidence that would help distinguish the explanations.
questions.model: If intermediate deposits or fossils are missing, forms sampled before and after the gap may appear to change abruptly even if change occurred over a longer interval. Researchers can examine better-sampled sites, date additional horizons and compare geographical occurrences and measured characters. Consistent patterns across independent records are stronger evidence than a single gap. The conclusion should retain uncertainty about the unobserved interval rather than treating absence as a direct observation.
criteria: Explain a preservation or sampling gap.
Suggest additional samples, sites or dates.
Retain uncertainty rather than equating absence with a process.

summary: Stasis concerns measured morphology, not necessarily genetic immobility.
Geological rapidity can span many generations.
Local gaps have several possible causes.
Tempo models must be tested for particular lineages and records.
sourceNotes: Clarification: punctuated equilibrium is not a replacement for natural selection or universally restricted to complex organisms.

title: Human Evolution
objectives: Place humans within primate and ape relationships.
Explain mosaic, branching evolution using anatomical and genetic evidence.
Distinguish biological and cultural evolution and evaluate claims about human variation.

glossary.definition: Here, a member of the human lineage after its separation from the lineage leading to chimpanzees and bonobos.
Different traits change at different times and rates.
Learning and passing information or practices between individuals rather than through DNA inheritance alone.

slides.title: Humans within primates
slides.html: Humans are primates and apes, not a group outside the animal evolutionary tree. Relationships are supported by combinations of anatomical and molecular evidence, rather than one feature that is absolutely universal in every primate. Grasping abilities, forward-facing eyes and flexible shoulders are useful comparative features, but each must be interpreted in the context of variation, specialisation and shared ancestry.

slides.title: Hominids and hominins
slides.html: Hominidae includes the great apes, including humans. In this lesson, hominin refers to the human lineage after separation from the lineage leading to chimpanzees and bonobos. This distinction prevents confusion between a broad ape family and the more restricted human branch. Living chimpanzees are relatives with their own evolutionary history, not unchanged versions of the ancestor from which humans evolved.

diagram.caption: Simplified relationship among these African-ape lineages. Branch tips are living lineages; the diagram does not show one living species turning into another or include all apes.

slides.title: A branching fossil history
slides.html: The human fossil record includes multiple lineages, some overlapping in time and region. It is not a sequence in which each named species necessarily replaced the previous one or directly produced the next. Fragmentary preservation and variation make some classifications uncertain. A fossil can support a particular combination of traits without establishing that its population was a direct ancestor of living humans.

slides.title: Mosaic anatomical change
slides.html: Habitual bipedalism, changes in teeth and jaws, body proportions and brain organisation did not all appear together. Different anatomical systems changed at different times, and early members of the human lineage did not necessarily have the large brains of recent humans. Analyse each trait with its evidence rather than assigning a single advanced or primitive ranking to the whole organism.

diagram.caption: General schematic teaching anatomy, not a reconstruction of a named hominin. Different regions provide different evidence about locomotion, diet and body proportions.

slides.title: Modern human origins
slides.html: Current fossil evidence places early Homo sapiens in Africa by about 300,000 years ago, rather than treating 200,000 years as a fixed earliest date. The emergence of the full combination of modern traits was complex and extended over time. Dates and classifications remain evidence-based estimates that can be revised by new specimens, improved dating and comparisons among populations.

slides.title: Biological and cultural evolution
slides.html: Biological evolution concerns inherited population change across generations. Cultural change involves learned information, practices and technologies being transmitted socially. Other animals also learn and use tools, so tool use alone is not uniquely human. Human cumulative culture can substantially alter environments and selection pressures, but it does not make biological inheritance or evolutionary processes cease to operate.

slides.title: Humans continue to evolve
slides.html: Mutation introduces genetic variants, gene flow moves variants among populations, drift changes frequencies through sampling and selection can affect reproductive contribution. Medicine, agriculture and transport change the conditions under which these processes operate; they do not place humans outside evolution. An individual’s increased lifespan or a population’s technological change alone is not proof of a particular allele-frequency trend.

slides.title: Interpreting human genetic variation
slides.html: Human genetic variation is overlapping and shaped by ancestry, migration and interbreeding. Patterns of geographical ancestry do not justify ranking people or treating broad racial labels as discrete biological subspecies. A DNA marker provides information about particular inherited variation, not a complete description of identity, behaviour or health. Claims about population differences must distinguish measured genetic patterns from unsupported social or deterministic conclusions.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes humans and chimpanzees?
options: Humans evolved from living chimpanzees.
They are separate living lineages sharing an earlier common ancestor.
Chimpanzees have not evolved since the lineages separated.
Humans are not apes.
feedback: The common ancestor was not a modern living chimpanzee.
Both lineages have their own subsequent evolutionary histories.
The chimpanzee lineage has continued evolving.
Humans are included within apes.
questions.explanation: Both lineages have their own subsequent evolutionary histories.

questions.prompt: What does mosaic evolution mean in a hominin context?
options: All human traits arose simultaneously.
Every fossil species is a direct ancestor of the next.
Different traits changed at different times or rates.
Brain size alone ranks every species in a progress sequence.
feedback: The anatomical changes were not one simultaneous package.
Branching histories do not establish a direct ancestor chain.
Mosaic evolution describes unequal timing among traits.
A single measure is not a universal rank of evolutionary progress.
questions.explanation: Mosaic evolution describes unequal timing among traits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about culture and biological evolution is most defensible?
options: Technology eliminates all mutation.
Medicine stops gene flow and drift.
Learning a skill necessarily changes the gamete DNA encoding it.
Culture can change selection pressures without stopping biological evolution.
feedback: Technology does not eliminate mutation.
Medicine does not abolish population processes.
Social learning is not the same as a directed gamete-DNA change.
Culture changes environments while inherited variation and population processes continue.
questions.explanation: Culture changes environments while inherited variation and population processes continue.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of broad geographical ancestry labels?
options: They do not capture all the overlapping genetic variation or determine a person’s complete identity.
They divide every human into perfectly separate subspecies.
They establish a ranking of intelligence without other evidence.
They prove all people within a labelled group have identical genes.
feedback: Ancestry patterns are partial information within a complex, overlapping history.
Human genetic variation does not form such perfectly discrete categories.
This is an unsupported deterministic and ranking claim.
Substantial individual variation exists within populations.
questions.explanation: Ancestry patterns are partial information within a complex, overlapping history.

questions.prompt: Explain why human evolution is better represented as a branching history than as a ladder from living apes to humans.
questions.model: Humans and other living apes are separate descendants of earlier shared ancestors, and each lineage has continued evolving. Fossil evidence also reveals several hominin lineages, sometimes overlapping in time, rather than one certain chain. Anatomical features changed at different rates, so no single scale ranks whole species from primitive to advanced. Branching models accommodate shared ancestry, divergence, extinct lineages and uncertainty about direct ancestral relationships.
criteria: Distinguish common ancestry from descent from a living ape.
Include multiple or overlapping fossil lineages.
Explain mosaic change or uncertainty rather than a progress ranking.

questions.prompt: Explain how cultural change can influence biological evolution without being identical to it.
questions.model: Cultural practices and technologies are transmitted through learning and can alter environments, diets, contact among populations and reproductive conditions. These changes can influence selection pressures or gene flow. Biological evolution, however, concerns inherited population change, not the learning process itself. Mutation and drift can continue as well. Showing that a practice changed therefore does not alone establish a specific genetic change; allele-frequency evidence is needed for that claim.
criteria: Distinguish social transmission from genetic inheritance.
Explain a route through changed selection pressures or gene flow.
Require genetic evidence for a specific biological-evolution claim.

summary: Humans are primates and apes with branching relationships.
Hominin traits evolved in a mosaic rather than as one package.
Early H. sapiens evidence extends to about 300 ka in Africa.
Culture changes evolutionary conditions but does not stop evolution.
Human genetic diversity does not justify rigid racial ranking.
sourceNotes: Corrected outdated source suggestion that culture lies outside selection models or that current human biological evolution is simply halted by medicine. Avoided obsolete genomic-project counts and deterministic racial categories.
